# Gastrinoma

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the stomach > Gastrinoma*

[Original Article Link](/library/QS0uz2)

---

## Summary

A gastrinoma (i.e., Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) is a <u>gastrin</u>-secreting <u>neuroendocrine tumor</u> and is most often located in the <u>duodenum</u> and <u>pancreas</u>. Most gastrinomas occur sporadically, but some are associated with other endocrine neoplasias (e.g., <u>pituitary adenomas</u>, <u>parathyroid adenomas</u>, <u>insulinomas</u>). More than half of all gastrinomas are malignant. Gastrinomas release high levels of <u>gastrin</u>, which stimulates the production of <u>gastric acid</u>. Patients typically present with recurrent, therapy-resistant <u>peptic ulcer disease</u> and <u>diarrhea</u>. Diagnosis is confirmed by findings of a <u>fasting</u> gastric <u>pH</u> ≤ 2 and <u>fasting</u> serum <u>gastrin</u> (FSG) > 1,000 pg/mL. In case of diagnostic uncertainty after initial testing, a <u>secretin stimulation test</u> is obtained. The primary objectives of management are controlling acid hypersecretion and managing the <u>malignant tumor</u>. <u>Proton pump inhibitors</u> (<u>PPIs</u>) are the preferred therapy to control acid secretion. Surgical <u>tumor</u> resection is indicated in patients with localized disease. <u>Chemotherapy</u> and radiation may be considered in advanced disease.

---

## Etiology

* Gastrinomas are assumed to arise from endocrine cells of the gut (mostly the <u>duodenum</u>) or the <u>pancreas</u>.

* Most gastrinomas occur sporadically (∼ 75% of cases). [[2]](/library/fZXka9)

* Some gastrinomas occur in association with <u>multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1</u> (<u>MEN 1</u>) (∼ 25% of cases). [[2]](/library/fZXka9)





References:[[3]](/library/U30b3f)[[4]](/library/p30Ljf)[[5]](/library/L60wlS)

---

## Pathophysiology

* Gastrinomas are <u>neuroendocrine tumors</u> of the <u>GI tract</u> that secrete <u>gastrin</u>.

* Hypergastrinemia → stimulation of <u>parietal cells</u> → <u>gastric acid</u> hypersecretion, which leads to:

* <u>Peptic ulcer disease</u>

* Inactivation of <u>pancreatic</u> enzymes → <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>steatorrhea</u> → <u>malabsorption</u>

* ∼ 60% of gastrinomas are malignant (but slow-growing) [[6]](/library/2ZXTa9)





> [!TIP]
> Other causes of <u>hypergastrinemia</u> include <u>PPI</u> use, <u>H. pylori</u> infection, <u>atrophic gastritis</u>, <u>chronic renal failure</u>, <u>vagotomy</u>, <u>gastric outlet obstruction</u>, <u>retained antrum syndrome</u>, and extensive <u>small bowel</u> resection. [[7]](/library/caWajP0)




References:[[1]](/library/o600NS)[[5]](/library/L60wlS)[[8]](/library/K60UNS)

---

## Clinical features

Most patients manifest with recurrent, therapy-resistant <u>peptic ulcer disease</u>.




* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* <u>Diarrhea</u> and <u>steatorrhea</u>

* <u>Dyspeptic</u> symptoms (e.g., <u>heartburn</u>)

* <u>Upper gastrointestinal bleeding</u>

* Weight loss

* Possible symptoms of other endocrine neoplasias (see <u>multiple endocrine neoplasias</u> for more information).





References:[[1]](/library/o600NS)[[8]](/library/K60UNS)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[9]](/library/WZXP09)[[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)[[11]](/library/PYWW6P0)




* Consider gastrinoma in patients with recurrent, therapy-resistant <u>PUD</u>, <u>GERD</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>, and/or <u>diarrhea</u>.

* Obtain FSG and gastric <u>pH</u> levels in all patients.

* If initial studies are inconclusive, order a <u>secretin stimulation test</u> or measure basal <u>gastric acid</u> output.

* After diagnostic confirmation:

* Assess for underlying <u>MEN 1</u> syndrome and other related conditions.

* Obtain <u>EGD</u> and abdominal imaging to localize the gastrinoma and assess for <u>metastases</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> To reduce the risk of severe complications of acid hypersecretion and <u>peptic ulcer disease</u>, avoid abruptly stopping <u>PPIs</u> when adequate coverage with <u>H2RAs</u> and/or <u>antacids</u> is unavailable. [[12]](/library/1aW2jP0)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[7]](/library/caWajP0)[[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)




#### Confirmatory studies




Consider stopping <u>acid suppression medications</u> prior to testing, if safe to do so.  [[11]](/library/PYWW6P0)




* <u>Fasting</u> serum <u>gastrin</u> (FSG) and gastric <u>pH</u> (initial studies) ;  [[12]](/library/1aW2jP0)

* FSG > 1,000 pg/mL and gastric <u>pH</u> < 2: gastrinoma is confirmed. [[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)

* FSG 101–1000 pg/mL and gastric <u>pH</u> < 2; : inconclusive result; perform a <u>secretin stimulation test</u>  [[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)

* Gastric <u>pH</u> ≥ 2: gastrinoma is unlikely  [[7]](/library/caWajP0)

* <u>Secretin stimulation test</u>

* Indication: inconclusive results of initial studies

* Mechanism [[12]](/library/1aW2jP0)

* In healthy individuals, an infusion of <u>secretin</u> inhibits <u>gastrin</u> secretion.

* In individuals with gastrinoma, <u>secretin</u> infusion causes a dramatic increase in <u>gastrin</u> secretion.

* Findings

* ↑ Serum <u>gastrin</u> by > 120 pg/mL over baseline FSG confirms gastrinoma  [[9]](/library/WZXP09)[[12]](/library/1aW2jP0)

* <u>False positives</u> may occur due to secondary <u>hypergastrinemia</u> (e.g., <u>H. pylori</u> infection, chronic <u>PPI</u> use).   [[13]](/library/QYWuKP0)

* Basal acid output  [[9]](/library/WZXP09)

* Indication: <u>secretin stimulation test</u> is unavailable or unreliable (e.g., due to <u>PPI</u> use)

* Findings: Basal acid output > 15 mEq/h suggests gastrinoma [[9]](/library/WZXP09)





> [!TIP]
> When it is safe to do so, stop <u>acid suppression medications</u> prior to performing confirmatory studies (<u>PPIs</u>: ≥ 1 week before; <u>H2 receptor blockers</u> (<u>H2RAs</u>): ≥ 24 hours before). [[11]](/library/PYWW6P0)




#### Follow-up studies




If gastrinoma is confirmed, consider the following studies in consultation with a specialist (e.g., gastroenterology, <u>endocrinology</u>).




* Assessment for <u>MEN 1</u>, e.g.: [[9]](/library/WZXP09)[[14]](/library/maWVOP0)

* ↑ <u>Calcium</u> and <u>parathyroid hormone</u> levels: <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u>

* ↑ <u>Prolactin</u> level: <u>prolactinoma</u>

* Mutation of the <u>MEN1</u> <u>gene</u> on <u>genetic testing</u>

* Assessment for other hormonal syndromes (e.g., <u>diagnostics for Cushing syndrome</u>)  [[9]](/library/WZXP09)

* <u>H. pylori stool antigen test</u>





> [!TIP]
> Up to 50% of all patients with gastrinoma have concomitant <u>H. pylori</u> infection; <u>H. pylori</u> infection can also cause a <u>false positive</u> on <u>secretin stimulation test</u>. [[9]](/library/WZXP09)[[12]](/library/1aW2jP0)




### <u>Tumor</u> localization [[9]](/library/WZXP09)




#### <u>Esophagogastroduodenoscopy</u> (<u>EGD</u>) [[12]](/library/1aW2jP0)




* Indication: all patients with confirmed gastrinoma

* Goals

* Localize <u>tumor</u>(s)

* Rule out <u>H. pylori</u> infection and malignant <u>ulcers</u>

* Findings [[9]](/library/WZXP09)

* Single <u>duodenal ulcers</u> (most common) or multiple <u>ulcers</u> in atypical locations (e.g., <u>distal</u> <u>duodenum</u>, <u>jejunum</u>)

* Thick <u>gastric folds</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The presence of multiple <u>ulcers</u> in atypical locations (e.g., the <u>jejunum</u>) should raise suspicion of gastrinoma. [[15]](/library/6aWjlP0)




![Duodenal ulcers in gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)](media/gotxri75es46q9t0niitruop.jpg)

Duodenal ulcers in gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)




#### Imaging [[9]](/library/WZXP09)




Obtain <u>cross sectional imaging</u> and either PET/CT or <u>scintigraphy</u> in all patients with confirmed gastrinoma.




* Modalities

* CT or <u>MRI</u> abdomen with contrast

* Gallium <u>PET/CT scan</u> (preferred) or <u>somatostatin</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>scintigraphy</u> (<u>octreotide</u> scan)  [[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)

* <u>Endoscopic ultrasonography</u> (<u>EUS</u>) if PET/CT is not used  [[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)

* Findings [[7]](/library/caWajP0)

* <u>Duodenum</u> (∼ 70% of cases)

* <u>Pancreas</u> (∼ 25% of cases): typically the head

* <u>Ectopic</u> locations (5–15% of cases): e.g., <u>liver</u>, <u>stomach</u>, <u>ovaries</u>

* In approximately 50% of cases, the <u>tumor</u> has already <u>metastasized</u> at the time of diagnosis.





> [!TIP]
> Most gastrinomas are found in an area called the gastrinoma triangle. The superior vertex of the gastrinoma triangle is formed by the junction of the <u>bile</u> and <u>cystic ducts</u>, the <u>medial</u> vertex by the neck of the <u>pancreas</u>, and the inferior vertex by the third portion of the <u>duodenum</u>. [[9]](/library/WZXP09)

---

## Treatment

Gastrinomas are primarily managed by specialists (e.g., gastroenterology, oncology, <u>surgery</u>).




### Pharmacological therapy [[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)




* <u>Acid suppression medications</u>: indicated for all patients with gastrinoma

* First-line: <u>PPIs</u> (e.g., <u>omeprazole</u> DOSAGE)  [[9]](/library/WZXP09)

* Second-line: <u>H2RBs</u> (e.g., <u>famotidine</u> DOSAGE)

* <u>Somatostatin analog</u>:  (e.g., <u>octreotide</u>): consider in advanced disease  [[7]](/library/caWajP0)[[9]](/library/WZXP09)





> [!TIP]
> <u>PPIs</u> are preferred because of their long <u>half-life</u>. <u>H2RAs</u> should not be used for initial therapy because of very high and frequent dosing requirements (i.e., every 4–6 hours). [[9]](/library/WZXP09)




### <u>Surgery</u> [[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)




* Exploration <u>laparotomy</u>: all patients with sporadic gastrinomas to identify tumors not seen on imaging

* Resection considered for:

* Localized, sporadic gastrinomas

* Gastrinoma with <u>MEN 1</u> if <u>tumor</u> size is > 2 cm

* <u>Liver transplant</u>: considered for patients with <u>metastases</u> confined to the <u>liver</u> [[7]](/library/caWajP0)





### <u>Anticancer therapy</u> [[9]](/library/WZXP09)[[10]](/library/WaWPjP0)




Consider the following therapies in patients with advanced or refractory disease.




* <u>Chemotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>streptozocin</u>, 5-<u>fluorouracil</u>, <u>doxorubicin</u>)

* Radiation (e.g., <u>peptide</u> <u>receptor</u>-targeted <u>radiotherapy</u>)

* <u>Liver</u>-directed therapy (e.g., chemoembolization) in patients with <u>metastases</u> primarily in the <u>liver</u>





### Monitoring [[9]](/library/WZXP09)




Consider the following for patients with active nonmetastatic disease.




* Biochemical studies: every 3–12 months (i.e., levels of <u>gastrin</u>, <u>calcium</u>, <u>PTH</u>, <u>vitamin B12</u>)

* <u>Cross sectional imaging</u>: annually

* <u>Somatostatin</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>scintigraphy</u>: at least every 3 years
